k1321: <s0>Vlorë's Lungomare and Akërnia</s0> have roughly doubled in three years on the strength of a premise — that Vlorë's own airport would open and put the city on the direct-flight map — that still hasn't happened. This is the cleanest example on the whole coast of the "premium without the fact" pattern: the price already moved as if the catalyst had landed, so from here the upside only exists if the airport actually opens, while every further delay is a real, ongoing downside with nothing offsetting it.
k1322: Where the same data says the opposite: Vlorë's ordinary city
k1323: Underneath the Lungomare story sits a second Vlorë that the hype has mostly skipped: the ordinary residential city trades at roughly €800–1,000/m², a genuinely two-speed market where the tourist-facing strip has run far ahead of the zone locals actually live in. That gap is the investment case — not a bet on the airport, a bet that the ordinary city eventually reconnects with its own tourist-zone pricing the way it has in comparable Albanian cities.
k1325: Orikum sits beside a working marina with room to grow — 846 planned mooring spaces, per the marina's own infrastructure plan — how many are actually built isn't independently confirmed — and its lower price segment has already moved 63%, from €800 to about €1,300/m², evidence the re-rating is underway rather than speculative. At up to €1,500/m² near the top of that range, it's still priced well under Vlorë's tourist strip for a zone with a comparable long-term catalyst (marina development) actually under construction rather than merely announced.
k1326: One caveat worth naming: Vlorë's own marina project, the more prominent one in the city itself, carries real governance controversy — a concession deal that forgave roughly €23 million owed by the investor drew formal investigation coverage, separate from the physical construction, which is real and ongoing. That's a reputational and regulatory risk sitting alongside the genuine progress, not a reason to write off marina-adjacent zones entirely, but a reason to check a specific project's own paperwork rather than assume every marina story here is as clean as the concrete being poured.
k1327: The village resale play: Dhërmi and Himarë's back roads
k1328: Village resale stock in Qeparo and Vunë, inland from the resort-branded parts of Dhërmi and Himarë, runs €1,100–1,800/m² — cheap relative to the coastline it's near, and largely ignored by the boutique-resort marketing that dominates search results for both towns. The upside case depends on a specific, unfinished project: a second access road into the Riviera via the Vlorë river valley, whose second construction lot isn't yet dated. That's real, unpriced upside tied to a real dependency — not a guaranteed timeline, and worth checking the lot's actual status before treating the road as a given. <s1>Himarë's own title risk</s1> is a live issue further up this coast too, so the usual title-history check matters here as much as the price does.
k1329: What this means if you're actually choosing between these zones
k1330: The pattern across all five zones is consistent: price has already run ahead of confirmed fact in Ksamil and Lungomare/Akërnia, and it hasn't yet caught up to genuine, partly-confirmed catalysts in Vlorë's ordinary city, Orikum and the Riviera's village stock. <s1>The Airbnb-yield numbers behind all of this are worth reading on their own</s1>, and <s3>the same overpriced-zone list sits inside the wider national picture here</s3> — this article is the zoomed-in version of that flag, not a replacement for it.

k1349: City by city: what a short-term rental actually earns
k1365: Vlorë's figure is the country's cleanest data point — it comes from an AirDNA dataset covering all of 2023 rather than a marketing-page snapshot, and it holds up against the same source's own August peak (ADR ~€98, 70% occupancy). Durrës is measured by three different providers that don't agree with each other (annual income estimates range from €4,000 to roughly €9,000 for the same market), which is why it's presented as a range rather than a point figure — a wide range is more honest than a false-precision average.
k1366: Vlorë's lead isn't only a summer rate. The city runs a working port and a student population — put at roughly 84,000 by the 2023 census, a figure DomLivo hasn't yet cross-checked against INSTAT's own release — that keeps long-term rental demand alive through the months Airbnb goes quiet elsewhere on the coast; winter LTR rents there run €250–800 depending on the unit. That's a cushion Sarandë and Ksamil don't have: both empty out from November to March with nothing but Airbnb bookings to fall back on, which is part of why Vlorë's average income holds up better than a resort town's average, which is really just its August number wearing a full-year label.
k1368: Ksamil costs more per square metre to buy into than Sarandë, its neighbour six kilometres up the coast. It also earns less on Airbnb — $5,495 a year against Sarandë's $6,960 — while its listing supply grew <s1>86% in a single year</s1>. Higher entry price, lower return, and the fastest-growing glut of competing listings on the whole southern coast. If an "investment case" for Ksamil rests on Airbnb income, the numbers underneath it don't support the price being asked.
k1369: The 15% tax that changed the math in 2026
k1370: Since 1 January 2026, every short-term rental host declares income through the DIVA system by 31 March and pays a flat 15% on the amount <s1>after</s1> the platform's commission — with no deduction for cleaning, management or furnishing costs. <s3>The mechanics are shared with the wider property-tax picture</s3>: no NIPT business registration is required, the rule is identical for residents and non-residents, and the tax authority receives booking data directly from Airbnb and Booking.com, so informal declarations aren't a realistic option anymore. A non-resident needs an Albanian tax ID to file, which in practice means a local representative or accountant.
k1371: That 15% comes off every figure in the table above. Vlorë's €1,163 gross becomes roughly €990 net of tax alone, before management fees.

Vlorë wins on absolute euros per month; Durrës Plazh is the more defensible case on return relative to what you paid, and it's also the zone with the most independent data behind it rather than a single provider's estimate.
k1374: Winter is the part every one of these numbers hides. Sarandë and Ksamil both show occupancy in the high 30s to low 40s as an <s1>annual average</s1> — the real number is close to 100% in August and close to empty from November to March. Budget for that swing, not for the average.
k1375: The numbers above are gross, and gross isn't what lands in your account
k1376: Every figure in the table is what the listing earns before anyone gets paid to run it. A local property manager typically takes 20–25% of that for cleaning, guest communication and turnover — on top of the 15% DIVA tax above, not instead of it. Vlorë's €1,163 gross becomes closer to €740–790 once both come off, still the strongest number on the coast, just not the headline figure everyone quotes.
k1377: The top of the market looks nothing like the average. In Ksamil, villas with a pool earn $35,000–66,000 a year against the zone's $5,495 median — a 6–12× spread that says more about the property than the location.
